Not at all. To use the most recent poster child, from what I can piece together a distributed system wouldn't have saved Ashley Madison. Which, admittedly, becoming the new Godwin's Law. You don't need to figure out where the data is stored in a SQL Injection attack. You don't even need to know in what format- at least, not at first. In fact, all of the data breech exploits I've cleaned up after came from people who had no way of knowing where the data was stored, in what format, or by what kind of server. In one case, a blind SQL Injection attack managed to replace a site's entire product catalog. You don't need to know where it's stored. You need to exploit how the data is accessed.

But that's just data theft, which doesn't undermine the integrity of the host machine. Let's talk about some cleverer stuff. PHP is a particularly friendly language, which makes it both popular and insecure as all hell. And once you get a PHP site to run arbitrary code through one injection form or another- form posts, file uploads, etc, it's possible to send shell commands. Same goes with XSS/Script Injection attacks. You're not changing the code, you're exploiting it. A checksum won't pick up the problem because files aren't changing. And in a truly decentralized system, logging won't help much- at least, not in time to pick up the fact that there's a code exploit in progress.

Fact of the matter is that too many companies don't understand, or at least bother to use, secure development concepts. Nor to enough of them understand the damage that can be done through a poorly secured web application. Hosting arbitrary sites on your own machine is a ludicrous risk.

We should also jettison the assumption that there needs to be one standard for public and private data.

There are multiple standards. But like the proverbial horse and water, this doesn't guarantee the necessary results.

As someone who has been online for quite a bit now, and delved into a similar technology in the early 90's, I can tell you that if the entire internet were to move to this model of "content distribution", you'd end up with some major bottlenecks UNLESS you figure out a way for content to ONLY end up on machines with available CPU/RAM/HDD space. In other words, pretty much what we have now.

The other way of handling this would be to figure out a way to have hundreds of files encoded in a single chain, so that a single set of data could be used over and over for multiple files (similar to how some compression algorithms work). If a node requested newganghamchallenve.wav, it could download a tiny file that told it how to arrange/rearrange data within one of the downloaded data sets to obtain the information it wanted. Kindda like giving someone a map (large amounts of data), and telling them to only look in a certain grid, from a certain way, in a certain angle, and add a the letter "B" to the third building down the middle of the street. This is stuff that has already been done, btw... the problem with this approach is that it becomes VERY easy to trick to the computer to run a number of things since the entire file must be looked at prior to the system deciding how to handle it.
